summary.text: For exponents \(2,3,4\), the congruence of a decimal number modulo \(81\) in terms of its digit sum and weighted digit sum, applied also to its reversal, forces the digit sum to be divisible by \(3^n\); the digit bound then shows that any positive admissible number no larger than the corresponding all-nines candidate must itself have every digit equal to \(9\), proving minimality. For \(n=j+5\), repeating the block \(4899999987\) exactly \(3^j\) times gives a number whose reversal repeats \(7899999984\); both blocks are divisible by \(3^5\), the repetition factor is divisible by \(3^j\), and this \(10\cdot3^j\)-digit admissible number is strictly smaller than the \(27\cdot3^j\)-digit all-nines candidate.

full_proof.text:
Let \(\operatorname{rev}(m)\) denote the integer obtained by reversing the decimal digits of \(m\). For a positive integer \(q\), the definition of \(a(q)\) may be expressed as follows: among all positive integers \(k\) such that \(q\mid \operatorname{rev}(kq)\), choose the least \(k\), and put \(a(q)=kq\). Equivalently, whenever at least one such integer exists, \(a(q)\) is the least positive multiple \(m\) of \(q\) for which \(q\mid\operatorname{rev}(m)\). All the values of \(q\) used below have explicit admissible multiples, so the alternative value \(0\) in the definition never arises.

We prove that, for every \(n\ge 2\),
\[
 a(3^n)=10^{3^{n-2}}-1
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 n\in\{2,3,4\}.
\]

## 1. A decimal-digit lemma modulo \(81\)

Write the decimal digits of a positive integer \(m\), starting with the units digit, as
\[
(d_0,d_1,\ldots,d_{L-1}).
\]
Thus \(0\le d_i\le 9\), \(d_{L-1}\ne0\), and
\[
 m=\sum_{i=0}^{L-1}d_i10^i.
\]
Set
\[
 S=\sum_{i=0}^{L-1}d_i,
 \qquad
 H=\sum_{i=0}^{L-1}i d_i.
\]
For the reversed digit list, the corresponding weighted sum is
\[
 H^{\mathrm{rev}}=\sum_{i=0}^{L-1}i d_{L-1-i}.
\]
Changing the index in this last sum gives
\[
 H^{\mathrm{rev}}=\sum_{i=0}^{L-1}(L-1-i)d_i,

after which
\[
 H+H^{\mathrm{rev}}=(L-1)S. \tag{1}
\]

Because \(10=1+9\), the binomial theorem gives, for every \(i\ge0\),
\[
 10^i=(1+9)^i\equiv 1+9i\pmod {81};
\]
all terms involving \(9^2\) are divisible by \(81\). Consequently,
\[
 m\equiv S+9H\pmod {81}. \tag{2}
\]
Reversing the digits does not change their sum, and applying the same calculation to the reversed list yields
\[
 \operatorname{rev}(m)\equiv S+9H^{\mathrm{rev}}\pmod {81}. \tag{3}
\]
This remains correct even if the units digit of \(m\) is zero: reversal may then discard a leading zero, but that zero contributes nothing to the represented integer or to either digit sum.

We now extract the key consequence. Let \(0\le e\le4\), and suppose
\[
 3^e\mid m
 \quad\hbox{and}\quad
 3^e\mid\operatorname{rev}(m).

after (2) and (3), respectively. Since \(3^e\mid 3^4=81\), congruence modulo \(81\) preserves divisibility by \(3^e\). It follows that
\[
 3^e\mid S+9H,
 \qquad
 3^e\mid S+9H^{\mathrm{rev}}.

after adding these divisibilities and using (1), we obtain
\[
 3^e\mid 2S+9(H+H^{\mathrm{rev}})
      =S\bigl(2+9(L-1)\bigr). \tag{4}
\]
The second factor in (4) is congruent to \(2\pmod 3\), so it is relatively prime to every power \(3^e\). Euclid's lemma therefore gives
\[
 3^e\mid S. \tag{5}
\]
Thus, for powers of \(3\) no larger than \(81\), simultaneous divisibility of a number and its reversal forces the decimal digit sum to be divisible by that same power of \(3\).

## 2. A minimality criterion for all-nines numbers

Suppose that \(e\le4\) and that positive integers \(e,N\) satisfy
\[
 3^e=9N. \tag{6}
\]
We claim that there is no positive integer \(m\) satisfying all four conditions
\[
 m<10^N-1,
 \qquad 3^e\mid m,
 \qquad 3^e\mid\operatorname{rev}(m). \tag{7}
\]

Indeed, let \(L\) be the number of decimal digits of such an \(m\), and let \(S\) be its digit sum. Since \(m<10^N-1<10^N\), we have
\[
 L\le N. \tag{8}
\]
Every digit is at most \(9\), so
\[
 S\le 9L\le9N. \tag{9}
\]
On the other hand, the digit lemma (5) says that \(3^e\mid S\). Since \(m>0\), at least one of its digits is nonzero, so \(S>0\). Therefore \(S\) is a positive multiple of \(3^e=9N\), and hence
\[
 S\ge9N. \tag{10}
\]
Combining (9) and (10) forces
\[
 S=9N,
 \qquad L=N.

after all, an \(N\)-digit string whose digits are each at most \(9\) can have sum \(9N\) only if every digit equals \(9\). Thus
\[
 m=\underbrace{99\cdots9}_{N\text{ digits}}=10^N-1,

a contradiction to the strict inequality in (7). This proves the claim.

It follows in particular that if \(10^N-1\) itself and its reversal are divisible by \(3^e\), then
\[
 a(3^e)=10^N-1. \tag{11}
\]
To justify the minimality in the formulation using multipliers, write the candidate as \(k_0 3^e\). It is admissible by hypothesis. If a smaller positive multiplier \(k<k_0\) were admissible, then \(m=k3^e\) would be positive, divisible by \(3^e\), would have reversal divisible by \(3^e\), and, because \(3^e>0\), would satisfy \(m<k_0 3^e=10^N-1\). This is exactly what the preceding argument rules out.

## 3. The exponents \(2,3,4\)

We apply (11) three times.

* For \(e=2\), take \(N=1\). Then
  \[
  3^2=9=9N,
  \]
  and \(10^N-1=9\). Its reversal is again \(9\), and \(9=3^2\). Hence
  \[
  a(3^2)=a(9)=9=10^{3^{2-2}}-1.
  \]

* For \(e=3\), take \(N=3\). Then
  \[
  3^3=27=9N,
  \]
  while
  \[
  10^N-1=999=27\cdot37.
  \]
  The number \(999\) is unchanged by reversal. Therefore
  \[
  a(3^3)=a(27)=999=10^{3^{3-2}}-1.
  \]

* For \(e=4\), take \(N=9\). Then
  \[
  3^4=81=9N,
  \]
  and
  \[
  10^N-1=999999999=81\cdot12345679.
  \]
  This number too is unchanged by reversal. Consequently,
  \[
  a(3^4)=a(81)=999999999=10^{3^{4-2}}-1.
  \]

This proves the desired equality for all three exponents \(n=2,3,4\), including the minimality assertion implicit in \(a\).

## 4. A family of smaller admissible multiples for every \(n\ge5\)

It remains to show that equality fails for every larger exponent. Begin with the 10-digit block
\[
 B=4899999987.
\]
Its decimal reversal is
\[
 R=7899999984.
\]
Both are divisible by \(3^5=243\); explicitly,
\[
 B=243\cdot20164609,
 \qquad
 R=243\cdot32510288. \tag{12}
\]

For \(j\ge0\), define
\[
 c_j=\sum_{i=0}^{3^j-1}10^{10i}. \tag{13}
\]
Multiplication by \(c_j\) repeats a 10-digit block exactly \(3^j\) times. Set
\[
 X_j=Bc_j. \tag{14}
\]
Since the shifted copies \(B10^{10i}\) occupy disjoint blocks of ten decimal positions, no carrying occurs between them. Thus \(X_j\) is the decimal integer obtained by writing \(B\) exactly \(3^j\) times in succession. In particular, it has exactly
\[
 10\cdot3^j \tag{15}
\]
decimal digits. Reversing a concatenation reverses the order of the blocks and reverses each block. Since every block here is the same, reversing their order has no effect, and hence
\[
 \operatorname{rev}(X_j)=Rc_j. \tag{16}
\]
There is no leading-zero issue: \(B\) begins with \(4\) and ends with \(7\), so the reversed block \(R\) also has ten digits.

We next prove
\[
 3^j\mid c_j. \tag{17}
\]
The sums (13) satisfy the recursion
\[
 c_0=1,
 \qquad
 c_{j+1}=c_j\bigl(1+10^{10\cdot3^j}+10^{20\cdot3^j}\bigr). \tag{18}
\]
Indeed, the \(3^{j+1}\) summands in (13) split into three consecutive groups, each containing \(3^j\) summands; the second and third groups are the first group shifted by \(10\cdot3^j\) and \(20\cdot3^j\) decimal positions, respectively.

For every \(K\ge0\), because \(10\equiv1\pmod3\),
\[
 1+10^K+10^{2K}\equiv1+1+1\equiv0\pmod3. \tag{19}
\]
Starting from \(c_0=1\), equations (18) and (19) show inductively that each passage from \(c_j\) to \(c_{j+1}\) supplies one additional factor of \(3\). Hence \(3^j\mid c_j\), proving (17).

Combining (12), (14), and (17), we find
\[
 3^{j+5}=3^5 3^j\mid Bc_j=X_j. \tag{20}
\]
Likewise, using (12), (16), and (17),
\[
 3^{j+5}\mid Rc_j=\operatorname{rev}(X_j). \tag{21}
\]
Therefore \(X_j\) is an admissible positive multiple in the definition of \(a(3^{j+5})\). By minimality of \(a\),
\[
 a(3^{j+5})\le X_j. \tag{22}
\]

It remains to compare \(X_j\) with the proposed all-nines value. From (15),
\[
 X_j<10^{10\cdot3^j}. \tag{23}
\]
But
\[
 10\cdot3^j<27\cdot3^j=3^{j+3}. \tag{24}
\]
Since powers of \(10\) are strictly increasing, (23) and (24) imply
\[
 X_j<10^{3^{j+3}}-1. \tag{25}
\]
For completeness, the subtraction of \(1\) causes no problem: the exponent on the right of (24) is strictly larger, so \(10^{3^{j+3}}-1\) is still larger than \(10^{10\cdot3^j}\), and hence larger than \(X_j\).

Together, (22) and (25) give the strict estimate
\[
 a(3^{j+5})<10^{3^{j+3}}-1. \tag{26}
\]
Now every \(n\ge5\) has the form \(n=j+5\) with \(j=n-5\ge0\), and then
\[
 n-2=j+3.
\]
Thus (26) becomes
\[
 a(3^n)<10^{3^{n-2}}-1
 \qquad(n\ge5). \tag{27}
\]
In particular, the conjectured equality is false for every \(n\ge5\).

Finally, an integer \(n\ge2\) is either \(2\), \(3\), \(4\), or at least \(5\). The three computations in Section 3 prove the equality in the first three cases, while (27) disproves it in the last case. Therefore
\[
 a(3^n)=10^{3^{n-2}}-1
 \quad\text{if and only if}\quad
 n\in\{2,3,4\},

after all \(n\ge2\), as required.
